result.summary: Pausanias notes the bare statue bases of Philopoemen at Megalopolis and sketches his life: his upbringing, character and model Epaminondas. He then recounts his early deeds: saving the Megalopolitans from Cleomenes, fighting at Sellasia, serving in Crete, and winning a cavalry victory at the Larisus.

scenes.title: Statue bases at Megalopolis
scenes.summary: Near the market-place stand a theatre and the bases of vanished bronze statues, one inscribed as Philopoemen's.

scenes.title: Philopoemen's youth and character
scenes.summary: Orphaned young, Philopoemen was raised by Cleander and taught by tutors. He was strong, plain, fond of farming, hunting and reading, and modelled himself on Epaminondas, though hot-tempered.

scenes.title: Cleomenes takes Megalopolis
scenes.summary: Philopoemen leads most of the people to safety in Messene and persuades them to return only with arms, not under a treaty.
scenes.stakes: The survival and freedom of the citizens of Megalopolis.

scenes.title: Battle of Sellasia
scenes.summary: Philopoemen fights on foot, is speared through both thighs, and survives. Antigonus admires him and invites him to Macedonia.
scenes.stakes: Philopoemen's life from a severe wound in battle.

scenes.title: Crete and cavalry command
scenes.summary: He declines Antigonus, serves as a mercenary captain in Crete, then returns and makes the Achaean cavalry the best in Greece.

scenes.title: Victory at the Larisus
scenes.summary: Philopoemen kills the Elean cavalry commander Demophantus and routs the Aetolian and Elean horse.
scenes.stakes: Victory for the Achaeans against Elis and the Aetolians.

notable_quotes.reason: Shows Philopoemen's ideal of emulating Epaminondas, the model for his career.

analysis.text: Pausanias presents Philopoemen as a Greek hero shaped by education and by a model, Epaminondas, yet limited by his temper.
The passage reflects Arcadian resistance to Sparta and the Achaean League's wars in the third century BC.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes the statues are gone and only inscribed bases remain, a sign of how much he relied on inscriptions.

language_notes.text: An elegiac couplet is a two-line verse form, a hexameter followed by a pentameter, commonly used for inscriptions.
"On a footing of old friendship" means Cleander and Craugis' family were long-standing friends.
Sophists were professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy; here the term simply means notable learned writers.
Returning "with arms in their hands" means as free, armed men, not as subjects accepting terms from Cleomenes.
"Fall forwards... the spear snapped off": his fall onto his feet's momentum broke the shaft, leaving the head in his thighs, as sentence 13 shows.

context_notes.text: Epaminondas was the Theban general who defeated Sparta at Leuctra and helped found Megalopolis; he was a model of virtue and generalship.
Cleomenes was the Spartan king who seized and sacked Megalopolis in 222 BC; Messene was an ally of the Arcadian city.
Sellasia (222 BC) was the battle where Antigonus of Macedonia and the Achaeans defeated Cleomenes of Sparta.
The Aetolians were rivals of the Achaean League, and Elis was allied with them against the Achaeans.

literary_notes.text: Philopoemen's emulation of Epaminondas shows his ideals, while the admitted shortfall makes him a more human figure.
The contrast between Epaminondas' mildness and Philopoemen's hot temper sharpens the comparison and names his flaw.
The brisk summary compresses years of achievement into one plain statement, typical of Pausanias' economical reporting.
